title: The Sociology of Moral Progress
paragraphs: Sociologists examining historical moral progress, including expanding circles of moral concern across previously excluded groups, increasingly question whether such changes reflect genuine moral discovery, uncovering previously obscured moral truths, or merely contingent shifts in social consensus lacking privileged epistemic status over historically preceding moral frameworks.

This question carries substantial implications for how contemporary societies should regard their own current moral commitments, since if historical moral change primarily reflects contingent social shift rather than genuine discovery, confidence in current moral frameworks representing genuine progress rather than merely contemporary contingent consensus becomes considerably less secure.

Some philosophers defend moral realism regarding historical progress, arguing that expanding moral circles genuinely track objective moral truths previously obscured by historically contingent biases and limited perspective, analogous to how scientific progress genuinely discovers objective truths previously obscured by limited historical understanding.

Critics counter that this moral realist framing imposes retrospective narrative coherence onto historical moral change that may more accurately reflect contingent social, economic, and political factors rather than genuine convergence toward objective moral truth existing independent of particular historical social conditions.

This disagreement between moral realist and constructivist interpretations of historical moral change reflects deeper unresolved metaethical questions regarding whether moral truth exists independent of social consensus or represents something more fundamentally constructed through evolving social agreement and consensus.

Given this persistent metaethical uncertainty, perhaps the most defensible practical stance combines genuine epistemic humility regarding whether current moral commitments represent final moral truth, with continued serious commitment to those principles judged most defensible through careful, ongoing moral reasoning and reflection.
